opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's an idea I keep coming back to, because the intuition is so appealing. A huge fraction of what a large model stores in its weights looks like lookup: local co-occurrence statistics, common phrases, facts that tend to show up in fixed surface forms. Spending dense matrix multiplies, on every token, to recover something a hash table could hand you almost for free feels wasteful. So the pitch is: offload that rote memorization into a big, sparse, cheap-to-access N-gram memory, and let the transformer parameters focus on composition and reasoning.

When you actually pursue it, a few things become clear.

First, there is real signal there. Injecting N-gram information as a side input, as embeddings keyed by hashed N-grams and added into the residual stream, does help. Especially at smaller scales or lower compute budgets, you see better quality per FLOP. The memory is nearly free at inference in compute terms. It costs memory bandwidth and capacity rather than arithmetic, and that's a nice trade on modern hardware where FLOPs are precious.

Second, "replacing" is a stronger word than the evidence supports. In my experience it behaves more like a complement than a substitute. The gains tend to shrink as the dense model gets bigger and better trained, because the transformer learns those local statistics anyway. And it learns them in a contextualized way that a fixed N-gram key can't capture. An N-gram doesn't know what the document is about. Attention does. So you get a nice boost early, but it doesn't scale as a one-for-one swap of parameters.

Third, the systems side matters as much as the modeling side. Huge embedding tables mean sharding, hash collisions, deciding which N-grams deserve slots, and keeping lookups fast in a serving stack that was built around dense compute. A lot of ideas that look good on paper die there. It's not that they're wrong. They just don't compose cleanly with everything else you're optimizing.

So where I've landed is that the promise is real but narrower than the headline. Separating "memory" from "computation" in these models is a direction I believe in. Whether the right memory is literally N-gram tables, or something more learned and retrieval-like, is still open. I see N-gram memory as a useful existence proof that cheap sparse lookup can buy you quality. The more interesting question is what the general version of that looks like at frontier scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that I went into it more excited than I came out, but not disappointed, if that makes sense.

The appeal is obvious when you look at what a transformer actually spends its parameters on. A huge fraction of the model is effectively memorizing: facts, phrases, surface-level co-occurrence statistics. That's expensive to store in dense weights, it's expensive to update, and every one of those parameters gets touched on every forward pass whether it's relevant or not. An N-gram table is the opposite. It's cheap, it's sparse, lookup is close to free, and you can scale it to trillions of entries without touching your compute budget. So the pitch was: let the table handle the memorization, and let the neural network handle the reasoning and composition. In principle you shrink the dense model, you get something you can inspect and edit, and you get a quality bump essentially for free.

And some of that held up. When we added large-scale N-gram lookups as an input feature, we did see real gains, especially at smaller model sizes, and especially on things like rare entities and long-tail knowledge. The engineering was also more tractable than I expected. Hashing a few billion N-grams into an embedding table and training it jointly is not exotic.

Where I became more sober is in two places. First, the gains compress as the dense model gets bigger. A large enough transformer is already a very good N-gram model, and it learns a smoothed, generalizing version rather than a brittle exact-match one. So the delta you get from the table shrinks right as you'd want it to matter most. Second, the "replace parameters" framing turned out to be too strong. You don't really get to remove transformer capacity and swap in a table one-for-one. The table is additive. It helps the model, but the model still needs most of its parameters to use the table well, to disambiguate, to compose, to know when the lookup is noise. Memory and computation are not as separable as the clean story suggests.

The other practical thing is that N-grams are a pretty crude key. Exact token sequences are a poor proxy for meaning. A lot of the later retrieval work, with learned dense keys, is really the same instinct pursued with a better addressing mechanism, and I think that's the right evolution of the idea.

So my view now is that the promise is real but narrower than the headline. It's a strong tool for efficiency at a given quality level, for long-tail knowledge, and for anything where you want to update facts without retraining. It is not a path to making the transformer dramatically smaller. I still think the underlying question, how much of a model should be dense compute versus external memory, is one of the most important open design questions we have. N-grams were just the first and simplest way to poke at it.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s something compelling about separating memorization from computation. We use these enormous parameter matrices both to store information and to do reasoning, and it’s natural to ask whether some of that information could live in a much cheaper lookup table. An N-gram memory is one way to explore that.

But I’d be careful about calling it a replacement for transformer parameters. A lookup can help when you encounter a familiar pattern; the harder question is what happens when the context changes or you need to generalize beyond that pattern. And the memory isn’t free—you have to retrieve it efficiently and make good use of it.

So I see the promise more as a complementary mechanism: let memory handle some of the recurring patterns, and let the network spend its capacity on computation. The test is whether that gives you better quality for the same total cost, rather than simply moving parameters somewhere else.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the promise is that you don’t necessarily need to use expensive computation to store every piece of information a model needs. Some of that information could live in a memory that you look up using the recent context—an N-gram—and then combine with what the transformer computes.

The appealing part is that you can grow that memory without increasing computation in the same way you would by making the transformer larger. But I’d be careful about calling it a replacement for transformer parameters. A lookup can give you information associated with a particular pattern; the harder question is how well that information generalizes and how the model uses it in a new context.

So I see it as a promising complement. The question is how much capacity you can move into memory while preserving the capabilities you care about, and whether the whole system is actually more efficient once you account for retrieving that memory.
